<reason>PRO (B) built a clean, stable frame—subsidies pay by fuel burned and cannot reach the vehicle-less poor, a design flaw versus CON's implementation risks—and held it through every round. B answered both pressure questions directly with A1/A2 (sanctions-driven erosion, 2019 repeat bargain; three concrete sources of savings including excluding the top via existing vehicle/payroll records), turned CON's "inefficient, yes" concession, and seized CON's admission that the minister "borrows" in the crisis month. CON (A) had real, well-constructed arguments—built-in indexation, the "narrow later" tension with the motion, the fiscally-backwards sequencing point, and the organized-coalition answer to B's Q2—but its case ultimately asked the judge to keep a program it conceded misfires because a state might fail to run the alternative, and B's "a vote is a feature, not fragility" reframe blunted A's strongest remaining route. A also lost punchlines to clipping in all four speeches, including the closing. B made the decision easier; clear but competitive win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's pressure Q1 ("indexed for whom?") followed by the Rebuttal 2/closing sequence: CON conceded the minister borrows when oil doubles, and B converted that into "a loan taken out without a vote so the SUV's discount can double," while recasting the indexation vote CON feared as the first time anyone is asked whether the poor get more. It neutralized CON's best live argument on automatic protection.</best_rebuttal>
